slides.title: Reproduction combines development, motivation, and care
body: **Reproductive behavior** includes actions that contribute to finding a partner, mating, and caring for offspring. These actions depend on sensory information, the body’s reproductive condition, and previous experience. A hormone can change how strongly a social cue influences behavior without specifying every movement the animal performs.

The **hypothalamus** coordinates endocrine signals and motivated actions through several distinct cell populations. Some neurons control pituitary hormone secretion; others influence mating, social recognition, or caregiving. Their effects depend on their receptors and projection targets, so activating one hypothalamic population does not reproduce every aspect of a reproductive state.

Parental care can occur after pregnancy, after mating, or through experience with another animal’s offspring. These routes recruit overlapping mechanisms while differing across species. Human reproduction also involves personal decisions, social relationships, and cultural knowledge, which cannot be inferred directly from a rodent’s mating posture or pup-retrieval response.

slides.title: Gametes contribute one chromosome set to a new embryo
body: **Gametes** are reproductive cells: sperm and ova. They are produced through **meiosis**, a form of cell division that reduces the chromosome number. Fertilization combines a chromosome set from each gamete, restoring the paired organization found in most cells of the developing human body.

The usual human chromosome complements include XX and XY, although other complements and mosaic patterns also occur. A chromosome carries many genes, and those genes must be expressed in particular cells at particular times. Chromosome composition therefore begins a developmental process rather than directly specifying an adult’s behavior.

**Sex traits** include chromosomes, gonads, hormone production, internal ducts, and external anatomy. These features usually develop in coordinated patterns but can differ from one another. Describing the particular trait being measured is more informative than assuming that a chromosome label supplies every anatomical, endocrine, and psychological detail.

slides.title: Gonadal differentiation changes embryonic hormone signals
body: Early gonads contain cells capable of developing along different pathways. In a typical XY embryo, expression of the **SRY** gene helps initiate a testis-development program. SRY acts through other regulatory genes and changes cell differentiation; it is not itself a circulating hormone that travels to the reproductive ducts.

Developing testes contain **Sertoli cells**, which produce anti-Müllerian hormone, and **Leydig cells**, which produce testosterone. These signals act on different targets. Their coordinated actions help organize internal reproductive anatomy, while local hormone conversion and receptor function influence how other tissues respond during the same developmental period.

Ovarian development also requires active gene regulation and maintenance of ovarian cell identity. It should not be understood as the complete absence of a developmental program. Differences in a regulatory gene, a hormone-producing cell, or a target receptor can alter different components of reproductive development independently.

slides.title: Early ovarian follicles can follow different fates
body: An **ovarian follicle** contains an oocyte surrounded by supporting cells. A mouse study used tissue clearing and lineage tracing to follow early follicles through development. **Lineage tracing** permanently marks a cell population and its descendants, allowing later tissue organization to be related to an earlier developmental origin.

The earliest growing follicles occupied the ovarian medulla, the inner region of the ovary. Most of these first-wave follicles lost their oocytes rather than producing the first mature eggs. Their supporting cells did not all disappear at the same time, so loss of an oocyte did not eliminate every contribution of that follicle.

The researchers distinguished these early follicles from later follicles stored nearer the ovarian cortex. Three-dimensional imaging preserved their spatial arrangement, which a single thin section could miss. Position and developmental history helped separate populations that looked superficially similar when classified only by their current size or stage.

Original figure legend: Figure 1. Wave 1 follicles are remodeled prior to peri-puberty. ( A ) Schematic diagrams of fetal and postnatal ovaries at the indicated stages (E = embryonic day; P = postnatal day). Wave 1 follicles, located in the ovarian medulla (below the dashed line), retain bipotential pre-granulosa (BPG, green) cells and develop without delay. In contrast, cortical follicles, which become quiescent primordial follicles (wave 2), undergo replacement of BPGs by epithelial pre-granulosa (EPG, yellow) cells. This replacement is completed by P5. By P21 (3 wk), wave 1 follicles undergo atresia, characterized by oocyte loss. Germ cells/oocytes are shown in blue. Dashed line: medullary–cortical boundary. ( B ) Postnatal follicular developmental timeline: wave 1 antral follicles emerge by 3 wk ( Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C ); juvenile sexual development (peri-puberty) occurs at 4–5 wk; ovulation takes place around 7–8 wk. ( C ) Annotation of total follicles in P5 and P10 ovaries using Imaris software (gray spheres). Each follicle with a DDX4-positive oocyte was manually counted and labeled using the Imaris spot model. Scale bars: left, 50 µm; right, 70 µm. ( D ) Total follicle counts in P5 and P10 ovaries (mean ± SD;  N  = 3–4). ns, not significant. ( E ) Annotation of wave 1 follicles in P5 and P10 ovaries using Imaris software (gray spheres). Follicles with oocytes larger than 20 µm in diameter, primarily located in the medulla, are classified as wave 1 follicles at the indicated times. Each gray sphere represents one follicle. Scale bars: left, 50 µm; right, 70 µm. ( F ) Wave 1 follicle counts in P5 and P10 ovaries (mean ± SD;  N  = 3–4). ns, not significant. ( G ) 3D projection of the ovary at P14, reconstructed using the Imaris surface model. Scale bars = 50 µm. ( H ) Oocyte volume increase in wave 1 follicles over time (mean ± SD;  N  = 10). (Note: Nuclear volume is excluded, as DDX4 is a cytoplasmic protein.) ****p < 0.0001. ( I ) Representative images of ovaries at 4 and 5 wk. Left (4 wk): arrowheads indicate an atretic follicle with a distorted oocyte and disorganized granulosa cells; arrow indicates a developing healthy secondary follicle. Right (5 wk): arrowheads indicate degrading follicles at various stages; arrow indicates a developing healthy secondary follicle. Scale bars = 100 µm. ( J ) Wave 1 follicle remodeling, indicated by oocyte loss over time (mean ± SD;  N  = 3–4). Oocyte loss begins around 3 wk and continues through 5 wk, accompanied by granulosa cell disorganization and cell death. ns, not significant; **p < 0.01; ****p < 0.0001.

slides.title: Follicle loss can leave steroid-producing cells behind
body: **Atresia** is the breakdown of a follicle that does not complete maturation. In the mouse lineage-tracing study, many early oocytes degenerated while surrounding **theca cells** persisted. Theca cells contribute to steroid synthesis, allowing the remains of an early follicle to influence endocrine function after its reproductive cell has been lost.

Near puberty, retained theca and interstitial cells expressed genes needed for androgen production. A nearby boundary population of later follicles supplied many of the earliest mature oocytes. The source of steroid-producing tissue therefore differed from the source of most eggs released during the first reproductive period.

The study combined anatomical tracing with single-cell gene-expression measurements. These methods distinguished a cell’s location and ancestry from the enzymes it could express. An ovarian structure can consequently contribute to hormone production without surviving as an intact follicle capable of releasing a mature oocyte.

slides.title: Different hormones act on the two embryonic duct systems
body: Early embryos contain **Müllerian** and **Wolffian ducts**, two internal duct systems with different developmental possibilities. Anti-Müllerian hormone acts through its receptor to promote Müllerian regression in typical testicular development. Testosterone supports Wolffian structures, including the epididymis and vas deferens, when their cells can respond to androgens.

These two hormone actions are separable. **Androgen insensitivity** results from reduced or absent androgen-receptor function, so testosterone cannot produce its usual effects in target tissues. Anti-Müllerian signaling can remain active, producing an anatomical pattern that cannot be described simply as a shortage of every testicular hormone.

Conversely, disrupted anti-Müllerian signaling can permit Müllerian structures to persist despite androgen-supported development elsewhere. These developmental variations identify distinct receptor-controlled processes. They concern particular anatomical and endocrine features and do not determine a person’s gender identity, relationships, interests, or sexual orientation from anatomy alone.

slides.title: Local conversion of testosterone affects external anatomy
body: In developing target tissues, the enzyme **5α-reductase** converts testosterone into **dihydrotestosterone**, or DHT. DHT activates androgen receptors and contributes to differentiation of external genital structures. The amount of testosterone in circulation therefore does not, by itself, specify the androgen signal experienced by every tissue.

A change in 5α-reductase can alter external development while leaving other testosterone-dependent processes relatively preserved. A change in the androgen receptor affects the ability to respond to either androgen. Distinguishing hormone synthesis, local conversion, and receptor activation helps explain why developmental variations can produce different anatomical combinations.

Puberty changes the endocrine environment again, and some androgen-dependent features may develop more strongly at that time. Clinical assessment considers the individual’s anatomy, hormone responses, and preferences. A developmental mechanism explains a biological process; it does not justify predicting someone’s identity from a single enzyme or chromosome result.

slides.title: Reproductive hormone neurons must reach the forebrain
body: **Gonadotropin-releasing hormone**, or GnRH, is secreted by neurons that regulate pituitary reproductive output. During development, many of these neurons originate outside the forebrain and migrate inward along nasal-associated pathways. Their final position depends on developmental signals that guide movement and interactions with neighboring axons.

A study of anti-Müllerian hormone signaling found its receptor in developing GnRH-related pathways. Mice lacking normal receptor function showed disturbed olfactory organization and GnRH-neuron migration. The hormone system associated with reproductive duct development therefore also had a separate developmental role in organizing a brain endocrine population.

Cleared-embryo imaging allowed the investigators to examine these pathways in three dimensions. Misplaced or missing GnRH neurons can reduce later reproductive signaling even when gonads are present. This developmental defect lies upstream of the adult pituitary and gonadal responses that would normally follow a hypothalamic secretory signal.

slides.title: Developmental signals can affect puberty and fertility
body: **Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism** describes reduced gonadal function caused by insufficient stimulation from the brain–pituitary system. The anti-Müllerian signaling study identified variants in affected people and tested related mechanisms in cells and mice. The combined approach asked whether altered signaling could disrupt GnRH development rather than only describing a clinical association.

Receptor-deficient mice had fewer appropriately positioned GnRH neurons and impaired reproductive hormone output and fertility. Cell experiments also examined how altered hormone signaling changed neuronal movement. A developmental migration problem could consequently lead to an adult endocrine deficit, even though the original disturbance occurred long before puberty.

The clinical variants affected only a subset of people with the condition, which has several possible biological causes. A deficient hormone response can arise at the hypothalamus, pituitary, or gonad. Identifying the affected level distinguishes a failure to generate the command from a failure of the downstream tissue to respond.

slides.title: Hormones can organize circuits and activate existing ones
body: **Organizational effects** change the development or lasting structure of a tissue or circuit during a sensitive period. **Activational effects** change the operation of an existing system while a hormone signal is available. These terms describe the timing and persistence of an effect, rather than two completely unrelated kinds of hormone.

In classic rodent experiments, early androgen exposure altered later hormone-dependent mating responses. In adults, gonadal hormone removal and replacement changed the expression of behavior through already developed circuits. The outcome depended on both developmental history and the hormone conditions present when the animal was tested.

Adolescence can include further circuit maturation, so development is not restricted to prenatal life. Hormones can change transcription, synaptic function, and tissue responsiveness over several timescales. A behavioral change after hormone treatment therefore needs a defined age, treatment duration, and neural target to identify the process being altered.

slides.title: Estrogen receptors help mating circuits mature
body: A recent mouse study examined the **medial preoptic area**, or MPOA, across adolescence. The researchers removed **estrogen receptor α**, encoded by Esr1, from defined neuronal populations. This receptor binds an estrogen signal and can regulate gene transcription, changing which proteins a cell produces as it matures.

Removing Esr1 from inhibitory, GABA-releasing neurons disrupted the developmental progression of mating behavior in both sexes. Removing it from the tested glutamate-releasing population did not produce the same behavioral outcome. The relevant hormone effect therefore depended on which cells received the receptor manipulation, rather than on a uniform change throughout the hypothalamus.

The experiment separated a receptor’s role in a specific neural population from its effects elsewhere in the body. The MPOA contains several cell types involved in social behavior. A receptor expressed across a region can influence different actions through particular neurons and their targets, rather than through a single regional on–off switch.

slides.title: Hormones change a neuron’s transcriptional development
body: The adolescent MPOA study measured gene expression in individual cells at successive developmental stages. **Single-cell RNA sequencing** identifies the RNA molecules a cell contains, providing evidence about which genes it is using. Cells were grouped by expression patterns rather than treating every neuron in the preoptic area as equivalent.

GABAergic neurons containing Esr1 followed sex-dependent transcriptional trajectories across adolescence. Deleting the receptor before adolescence interrupted their normal progression through these gene-expression states. The receptor influenced the developmental program of these neurons, including coordinated changes across several genes rather than only one immediate electrical response.

The researchers also used tissue-based RNA detection to locate expression changes within the brain. Sequencing supplied molecular detail, while anatomical labeling retained spatial information. Together with the behavioral manipulation, these measurements related a defined receptor to the maturation of a particular cell population and the later expression of mating behavior.

slides.title: The reproductive axis uses a sequence of endocrine signals
body: The **hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal axis** begins with GnRH secretion into blood vessels that supply the anterior pituitary. GnRH activates receptors on pituitary **gonadotrophs**, cells that release luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone. These pituitary signals travel through the circulation to reproductive tissues rather than directly moving the muscles used in mating.

**Luteinizing hormone**, or LH, and **follicle-stimulating hormone**, or FSH, regulate gonadal steroid production and gamete development through different target cells. The resulting gonadal hormones feed information back to the brain and pituitary. Feedback changes subsequent secretion, allowing reproductive output to respond to the current state of the gonads.

The timing of GnRH release matters because repeated pulses and sustained exposure do not have identical effects on pituitary receptors. A blood hormone concentration is therefore only part of the signal. The frequency, duration, and biological target of a secretion pattern help determine what the downstream cells do.

slides.title: Kisspeptin circuits combine excitation and peptide feedback
body: **Kisspeptin** is a peptide that strongly excites the reproductive GnRH system. Many arcuate kisspeptin neurons also produce **neurokinin B** and **dynorphin**. A mouse brain-slice study used light-sensitive channels to stimulate these neurons and record the electrical responses produced in their local circuit and downstream targets.

High-frequency stimulation produced a slow excitatory response mediated by neurokinin signaling. Blocking the neurokinin receptor reduced that response, whereas activating a dynorphin-sensitive inhibitory pathway opposed it. Peptide release therefore provided interacting excitatory and inhibitory influences that could coordinate activity across the neuronal population.

The same study traced routes through which arcuate neurons could excite preoptic kisspeptin and GnRH neurons. Fast glutamate signaling and slower peptide signaling acted at different circuit steps. Coordinated endocrine output can consequently emerge from a network whose cells communicate through transmitters with different targets and response durations.

slides.title: Estrogen feedback differs across kisspeptin populations
body: An adult mouse experiment disrupted estrogen receptors separately in preoptic and arcuate kisspeptin populations. Targeting adults helped distinguish ongoing receptor action from an earlier developmental effect. The manipulation changed a hormone-sensing mechanism within an established circuit rather than removing the ovaries or every estrogen-responsive cell.

Reducing estrogen receptor function in preoptic kisspeptin neurons blunted LH surges and reduced neuronal excitability. Disrupting the receptor in arcuate kisspeptin neurons disturbed reproductive cyclicity and changed their synaptic input. The same receptor therefore contributed to different aspects of endocrine timing depending on its location.

**Positive feedback** strengthens output under the appropriate reproductive conditions, while **negative feedback** limits it. These effects require circuitry capable of interpreting a hormone signal differently across cell populations. A circulating estrogen increase does not produce the same electrical or secretory response in every kisspeptin neuron that encounters it.

slides.title: Follicles and pituitary signals change across the cycle
body: During the **follicular phase**, ovarian follicles grow under gonadotropin stimulation and produce increasing estradiol. **Estradiol** is an estrogen that acts in reproductive tissues and the nervous system. Its effects depend on concentration, duration, and cycle stage, including feedback onto the hypothalamic and pituitary cells controlling further secretion.

An LH surge contributes to **ovulation**, the release of an oocyte from a mature follicle. The remaining follicular tissue becomes the **corpus luteum**, which produces progesterone as well as estradiol. The endocrine contribution of the same ovarian structure therefore changes after the oocyte is released.

If pregnancy is not established, corpus-luteum support declines and ovarian steroid levels fall. The uterine lining responds to these endocrine changes, and another cycle can begin. Ovulation, steroid secretion, and uterine changes are coordinated events, but measuring one does not directly reveal the timing of every other component.

slides.title: Progesterone changes reproductive target tissues
body: **Progesterone** is a steroid hormone produced prominently by the corpus luteum after ovulation. It acts through receptors in reproductive tissues and the brain, contributing to changes appropriate to the luteal phase. Its effects depend partly on earlier estrogen exposure, which can change receptor availability and the condition of the target tissue.

In the uterus, ovarian steroids regulate the growth and maintenance of the endometrium, the internal lining. In the nervous system, hormone-sensitive circuits can alter physiological regulation and behavior. A change in circulating progesterone therefore acts on several targets, with different consequences according to each tissue’s receptors and ongoing state.

The familiar cycle diagram represents coordinated changes over time rather than a precise calendar shared by every person. Follicular timing and ovulation can vary. Hormone measurements, reproductive anatomy, and observed cycle events provide different evidence and should not be replaced by assuming that ovulation always occurs on one fixed day.

slides.title: Preoptic kisspeptin activity rises before the LH surge
body: A recent mouse study recorded calcium-dependent fluorescence from preoptic kisspeptin neurons across the estrous cycle. **Fiber photometry** collects light from a labeled neuronal population near an implanted optical fiber. The changing fluorescence reports population calcium activity rather than directly measuring GnRH secretion or the firing of every individual neuron.

On proestrus, the stage preceding ovulation, the researchers observed prolonged slow activity oscillations with faster transients superimposed. These patterns were much less evident at other cycle stages. Concurrent blood sampling showed that the beginning of the population activity preceded the peak of the LH surge rather than occurring only after it.

The onset varied across animals and across repeated cycles in the same mouse. The reproductive signal was therefore a sustained and temporally structured population event, not a single precisely timed spike. Comparing neural fluorescence with blood hormone measurements helped distinguish activity in the control circuit from the endocrine response it accompanies.

slides.title: Estrogen replacement restores a timed kisspeptin pattern
body: The preoptic kisspeptin study also removed the ovaries and replaced estradiol under controlled conditions. **Ovariectomy** removes an important source of ovarian hormones, allowing replacement experiments to ask which signals are sufficient to restore a particular neural pattern. The surgery also removes normal cyclic ovarian feedback.

Acute estradiol treatments did not simply generate the prolonged oscillatory pattern whenever they were given. The characteristic activity emerged during the expected surge period under the replacement regimen. The response depended on a prepared endocrine and temporal state, rather than on the immediate presence of estrogen alone.

These recordings distinguish a surge-associated preoptic population from the arcuate network involved in pulsatile reproductive output. Both use kisspeptin but have different activity patterns and feedback roles. A shared peptide name therefore does not imply that the two cell populations generate identical signals throughout the reproductive cycle.

slides.title: Human menstrual and rodent estrous cycles differ
body: A **menstrual cycle** includes cyclic changes in the uterine lining and its shedding when pregnancy is not established. Many laboratory rodents instead have an **estrous cycle**, with a shorter sequence of ovarian and behavioral changes. Their receptive period is more tightly restricted by the cycle than human sexual behavior generally is.

In rats, estradiol followed by progesterone can prepare and promote receptive mating responses. The same simple hormonal sequence does not determine human sexual choices or relationships. Human motivation is influenced by endocrine state together with learned expectations, health, personal meaning, social circumstances, and the presence of a desired partner.

A reproductive cycle is therefore different from a behavioral timetable. Ovulation concerns ovarian physiology, receptivity concerns the response to mating, and desire concerns motivation and experience. These processes can influence one another without occurring as an obligatory sequence whenever a particular hormone reaches a particular concentration.

slides.title: Pituitary cells can respond to metabolic signals
body: A zebrafish study examined how **cholecystokinin**, or CCK, influences reproductive hormone secretion. CCK is a peptide associated with nutrient signaling and satiety. The researchers found a CCK receptor in pituitary FSH cells, providing a route by which a metabolic signal could act directly on endocrine cells controlling ovarian development.

Calcium imaging showed that FSH cells responded strongly to CCK stimulation, whereas GnRH predominantly activated LH cells under the tested conditions. The response separated two pituitary populations often grouped together as gonadotrophs. Their shared reproductive function did not require identical sensitivity to the same upstream releasing signal.

Mutating the relevant CCK receptor impaired ovarian development and gonadotropin secretion. The physiological effect therefore extended beyond an isolated fluorescence response. This mechanism was established in fish; it should not replace the GnRH-centered organization of the mammalian reproductive axis without corresponding evidence from mammalian pituitary cells.

slides.title: Distinct secretory cells do not always share the same input
body: The zebrafish experiment compared LH and FSH cells while preserving their anatomical relationship in the pituitary. Fluorescent labels identified each population, and a calcium indicator tracked responses during stimulation. Nearby endocrine cells could consequently be monitored within the same tissue while their responses were assigned to different cell types.

GnRH evoked prominent activity in LH cells, while CCK recruited the FSH population more effectively. Receptor disruption also disturbed secretion, showing that cellular responsiveness and endocrine output had functional consequences. The investigators tested both the response to an applied signal and the effect of removing the signal’s receptor.

In an egg-laying species, growing the ovary and triggering ovulation impose different physiological demands. Separating FSH-related development from LH-related release permits different regulatory inputs to influence those processes. The result concerns the organization of this fish endocrine system rather than a universal rule that one peptide controls all vertebrate reproduction.

slides.title: Hormone receptors alter rodent mating circuits
body: In male rodents, testicular androgens help maintain mating motivation and performance through hormone-sensitive brain regions. Testosterone can act through the androgen receptor or be converted into estradiol by **aromatase**. The importance of each route depends on species, developmental stage, neural population, and the particular behavior being measured.

In female rats, estradiol followed by progesterone facilitates receptive behavior, including **lordosis**, a posture that permits mounting. Estradiol changes the readiness of the relevant circuit, including receptor expression, while later progesterone can promote its activation. Removing either the appropriate hormone signal or its neural target can impair the response.

A hormone-dependent mating response is still produced through sensory and motor pathways. The animal must detect a partner, evaluate contact, and organize posture and movement. Endocrine treatment changes the conditions under which those circuits operate; it does not substitute for every sensory event involved in the interaction.

slides.title: Estrogen regulates a reversible social peptide signal in fish
body: In medaka fish, researchers examined **neuropeptide B**, a signaling molecule expressed strongly in particular female brain regions. Its expression depended on estrogen-responsive DNA regulation. A receptor-bound hormone could therefore change the production of a peptide that subsequently acts on other cells within the social-behavior network.

Changing the adult steroid environment reversed the sex-biased expression pattern. This was an adult regulatory change rather than a permanent consequence of chromosome complement alone. The same brain could alter its peptide expression when the endocrine conditions changed, demonstrating substantial physiological flexibility in this particular fish system.

The investigators identified peptide-related expression in several brain and spinal regions relevant to social behavior. This distribution provided possible routes from estrogen-sensitive gene regulation to a coordinated behavioral response. The mechanism concerns neuropeptide expression and fish mating behavior and does not establish how human identity or orientation develops.

slides.title: Removing a peptide pathway changes female receptivity
body: The medaka neuropeptide B study tested behavior after disrupting the peptide genes or their receptor. **A knockout** removes normal gene function, allowing researchers to ask whether an intact pathway contributes to the measured response. They compared female responses to male courtship rather than assuming that altered RNA expression necessarily changed behavior.

Females lacking normal neuropeptide B signaling showed impaired receptivity to male courtship. The receptor manipulation and peptide manipulations affected different steps of the same signaling system. Their converging behavioral effects helped identify a pathway through which estrogen-dependent gene expression could influence a social response.

The original recordings show whole-animal interactions, while gene-expression and anatomical measurements identify candidate biological steps. These measurements answer different questions. A change in mating latency can reflect altered responsiveness within the interaction and should not be described as a direct measurement of a fish’s subjective experience or a human psychological category.

slides.title: Human sexual motivation has several interacting influences
body: Gonadal hormones contribute to human sexual function and motivation, particularly when endocrine function is markedly reduced. They act within a person who also has memories, preferences, relationships, and expectations. The same hormone concentration can therefore accompany different behavior depending on health, medication, personal experience, and social circumstances.

**Desire**, physiological arousal, and behavior are related but distinguishable processes. A change in genital response does not establish what someone wants, and a reported wish does not guarantee a particular physical response. Measurements need to specify whether they concern motivation, circulation, endocrine status, subjective experience, or an observed action.

Adult hormone treatment can alter the intensity of motivation without determining the sex or gender of a desired partner. **Sexual orientation** concerns patterns of attraction, not simply the amount of sexual interest. Evidence about changing hormone levels should therefore be interpreted at the level actually measured rather than extended automatically to partner preference.

slides.title: Brain estrogen strengthens androgen-dependent action
body: A medaka study removed the brain-enriched aromatase **Cyp19a1b**, which converts androgens into estrogens. Mutant males showed impaired mating and aggressive behavior despite elevated brain androgen levels. The behavioral deficit therefore could not be explained simply by assuming that the brain lacked every form of androgen signal.

Estrogen administration rescued the affected behaviors under the tested conditions. Molecular measurements indicated that brain-derived estrogen helped maintain androgen-receptor expression. Estrogen could consequently facilitate an androgen-dependent behavior by altering the receptor machinery through which another steroid acts, rather than replacing every downstream androgen action.

This mechanism differs from a simple division in which estrogens act only in females and androgens only in males. Both hormone classes can participate in the same male neural pathway. Their effects follow receptor expression, local synthesis, and cellular state rather than the everyday gender labels attached to the hormone names.

slides.title: One steroid can regulate the receptor for another steroid
body: The medaka aromatase study examined regulatory DNA associated with androgen-receptor genes. **Transcription** is the production of RNA from a DNA template. When estrogen receptors activate appropriate regulatory sequences, they can increase the RNA available for producing androgen receptors in a hormone-sensitive cell.

Experiments supported direct estrogen-sensitive regulation of androgen-receptor transcription. Different estrogen-receptor subtypes contributed to the expression of the two medaka androgen-receptor genes in relevant brain regions. The signal therefore changed the cell’s capacity to detect another hormone rather than merely adding a second independent excitatory input.

The resulting behavior depends on several steps: local estrogen production, estrogen-receptor action, androgen-receptor availability, and downstream androgen signaling. A deficit at the first step can weaken the final response even when androgen remains abundant. Measuring hormone concentration alone would miss the altered receptor availability within the receiving tissue.

slides.title: Sensory pathways carry social cues to reproductive circuits
body: Rodents obtain social information through odors, touch, vocalizations, and movements. The **main olfactory system** detects many volatile molecules, while the **vomeronasal organ** detects particular chemical cues through another sensory pathway. These systems send information through different routes that can converge on amygdalar and hypothalamic networks.

The **medial amygdala** receives important social chemosensory input and communicates with reproductive and defensive circuits. Its neurons do not simply label every encountered odor as a mating signal. Responses depend on the chemical pattern, the animal’s internal state, and previous experience with the individual producing the cue.

Sensory information must also be translated into a suitable action. Recognizing a conspecific’s odor is different from approaching, investigating, mounting, or caring for it. Reproductive circuits combine identity-related sensory input with hormone-sensitive motivation and motor organization before any particular social behavior appears.

slides.title: Oxytocin helps amygdala cells distinguish social cues
body: A mouse study investigated **oxytocin receptors** in the medial amygdala. Oxytocin is a peptide signal whose effects depend on the cells expressing its receptor. The researchers tested whether this signaling helped animals discriminate social cues from male and female conspecifics rather than treating oxytocin as a general increase in friendliness.

Reducing oxytocin signaling impaired the normal discrimination of these cues and altered social investigation. Receptor manipulation in aromatase-expressing neurons identified a specific cellular target within the medial amygdala. The behavioral effect therefore depended on oxytocin acting in a defined population involved in processing socially relevant sensory information.

Neuronal recordings showed changes in sex-biased responses to conspecific cues when oxytocin signaling was altered. The peptide changed how sensory information was represented by the circuit. It did not simply instruct the animal to perform one complete motor sequence irrespective of what social stimulus was present.

slides.title: Acute receptor blockade alters a sensory response
body: The medial-amygdala study combined developmental manipulations with acute inhibition of oxytocin signaling. **Acute inhibition** changes signaling during a relatively short experimental period. This approach asks whether ongoing peptide action contributes to a response after the sensory circuit has already developed, rather than only shaping its early construction.

Blocking oxytocin receptors altered social interaction preference and the neuronal response profile. Manipulating the oxytocin source also changed the discrimination pattern. These interventions acted at different points in the pathway, linking peptide availability and receptor activation to the operation of an established social-sensory network.

A behavioral preference in this assay describes investigation of particular mouse stimuli under controlled conditions. It is not a direct model of every aspect of pair bonding or human attraction. The neural result is that oxytocin can adjust the representation and behavioral influence of socially relevant cues within a defined amygdala circuit.

slides.title: Female mice use song timing when choosing an approach
body: Male mice produce sequences of ultrasonic vocalizations during courtship. A playback study asked which acoustic features female listeners used when approaching these sounds. **Playback** presents a controlled recording through a speaker, allowing investigators to change one feature while preserving much of the remaining sound rather than changing the live male.

Females preferentially approached intact songs over versions whose temporal regularity had been disrupted. The relevant information concerned how vocal events were distributed in time. Altering the rhythm changed the receiver’s behavior even though the sound still contained the kinds of syllables associated with the original courtship recording.

The experiment measured a movement toward a sound source, not mating success or a report of attraction. Speaker location and the animal’s tracked trajectory made the response observable. The finding identifies an acoustic feature that influences a social decision while leaving later partner interaction and reproductive outcome unmeasured.

slides.title: A signal can preserve syllables but lose its rhythm
body: The courtship-song study separately manipulated temporal regularity, syllable sequence, and the spectrotemporal structure of individual syllables. **Spectrotemporal structure** describes how sound frequencies change through time. These controlled changes tested whether the female response depended on a general distortion or on one particular property of the vocal sequence.

Approach behavior was more sensitive to disrupted temporal regularity than to the tested changes in syllable order or fine syllable structure. The female auditory system did not need to preserve every physical detail to treat the recording similarly. Different acoustic dimensions therefore had different behavioral importance in this particular social task.

Tracking the animal during repeated sound presentations also separated an initial position from a subsequent approach. The receiver extracted information from a time-varying signal and converted it into a movement decision. That transformation is one mechanism by which a partner’s behavior can influence reproductive interactions before direct physical contact occurs.

slides.title: Human chemical communication requires specific evidence
body: A **pheromone** is a chemical signal that produces a defined effect in another member of the same species under an established signaling system. Many rodent pheromone mechanisms are well characterized. Human odor communication is studied through different methods, and a laboratory response to an odor does not automatically establish a natural human pheromone.

Human studies may measure odor detection, mood, physiological responses, or judgments of social information. Each endpoint tests a different process. Demonstrating that an applied compound changes a judgment requires controls for smell intensity and expectations, but it still does not show that the compound governs natural partner choice.

The vomeronasal pathways central to many rodent experiments should not be assumed to operate identically in adult humans. Human social chemosensation can involve ordinary olfactory processing. Claims about endocrine modulation of an odor task must identify the actual stimulus, dose, population, and response measured rather than borrowing a rodent mating mechanism unchanged.

slides.title: A human odor study measured judgments of body motion
body: One human experiment tested whether steroid-like odor compounds changed judgments of **point-light walkers**, displays made from dots representing body joints. Participants classified the apparent sex-related characteristics of the moving figure. The task measured a perceptual decision about an ambiguous stimulus rather than choosing a real-life romantic or sexual partner.

The investigators combined odor presentation with intranasal oxytocin, vasopressin, or a receptor antagonist. Changes in the point where participants switched between response categories indicated altered perceptual judgments. Comparing treatments tested whether the peptide-signaling condition influenced the effect of the chemical stimulus on that specific task.

The study examined defined groups of men and controlled laboratory conditions. Its outcome concerns chemosensory modulation of a visual judgment, not a demonstrated universal human pheromone. A shift in an ambiguous classification task cannot establish that an odor changes someone’s sexual orientation or determines whom they desire.

Original figure legend: Figure 1. Experimental procedure and design. ( A ) Schematic illustration of a trial in the gender identification task. Each trial began with a 500 ms fixation cross, followed by a dynamic point-light walker (PLW) presented for 500 ms (0.5 walking cycle). Participants then pressed one of two buttons to indicate whether it was a male or a female walker. The physical gender of the PLW was denoted by a Z score and ranged in seven equal steps from feminine (−0.45 SD) to masculine (0.45 SD) with the center (0) individually adjusted to approximately perceived gender neutrality in the absence of drug treatment and olfactory stimulus. ( B ) Participants’ gender judgments for PLWs were fitted with a psychometric function that contained two parameters: point of subjective equality (PSE) and difference limen. The PSE is the physical gender of a PLW (Z value) that corresponds to a probability of 50% on the fitted psychometric function (gray circle on the x-axis), where the participant perceived the PLW as equally masculine and feminine. The difference limen is half the interquartile range of the fitted function. ( C ) Participants’ PSEs when smelling either chemosignal were compared with those when smelling the carrier control alone (gray circle). A negative PSE shift relative to the carrier control condition (dark gray arrow) corresponds to an overall leftward shift of the psychometric curve and reflects an increased tendency to judge the PLWs as male, hence a masculine bias in gender perception. Conversely, a positive PSE shift (light gray arrow) indicates a feminine bias in gender perception. All curves here are hypothetical. ( D ) Experiments 1 and 2 tested heterosexual and homosexual men, respectively. Drug treatment (60 µg atosiban, 24 IU oxytocin, 24 IU vasopressin) served as a between-subjects factor whereas olfactory condition (androstadienone, estratetraenol, carrier control) served as a within-subjects factor. Participants performed the experimental blocks of the gender identification task 35 min after nasal drug administration, under the continuous exposure of an olfactory stimulus. ( E ) Experiments 3 and 5 tested high AQ (AQ scores ≥ 25) and low AQ (AQ scores < 25) heterosexual men, respectively. Both drug treatment (no drug, 12 IU oxytocin, 24 IU oxytocin, 12 IU vasopressin, 24 IU vasopressin) and olfactory condition (estratetraenol, carrier control) were manipulated in a within-subjects fashion.

slides.title: Oxytocin effects can depend on dose and the measured task
body: The human chemosensory experiment found that oxytocin did not act as a simple dose-dependent gain knob. The perceptual effect varied nonlinearly with dose and differed across participant characteristics. **A nonmonotonic response** changes direction or relative strength across doses rather than increasing steadily whenever more of a compound is administered.

The antagonist **atosiban**, which can block oxytocin and vasopressin receptors, reduced the tested odor-related perceptual effects. Because the drug acts on more than one receptor system, its result does not isolate a single receptor subtype by itself. The comparison still identifies receptor-dependent modulation within the conditions of the experiment.

Intranasal administration, blood hormone concentration, and peptide action at a particular synapse are different measurements or interventions. This study manipulated administration and measured perceptual choices. It did not directly record peptide release in the human medial amygdala or demonstrate the rodent receptor-specific mechanism at the corresponding human cellular site.

slides.title: Preoptic and spinal circuits organize male mating responses
body: The **medial preoptic area** contributes to the sensory integration and motivation involved in male rodent mating. Its connections reach hypothalamic and brainstem regions that influence motor and autonomic output. Hormone receptors within this network alter its responsiveness to a partner and to genital sensory feedback during an interaction.

Spinal and brainstem circuits organize patterned components of copulation and ejaculation. Sensory input from the genitals can change the state of these circuits, while descending influences can facilitate or inhibit their activity. A coordinated mating response therefore requires communication across several levels of the nervous system rather than activity in the preoptic area alone.

Lesions, hormone replacement, and local stimulation answer different questions about the network. A lesion can establish that intact tissue contributes to normal performance, while stimulation can reveal actions the manipulated circuit can produce. Neither method by itself identifies every neuron normally active at each stage of the behavior.

slides.title: Female preoptic cells respond to events within mating
body: A mouse study followed female behavior and preoptic neuronal activity during a self-paced mating task. **Self-paced mating** allows the female to control aspects of access to the male. This arrangement distinguishes changes in her approach or contact behavior from a sequence imposed entirely by the experimenter or the male’s location.

The researchers observed heterogeneous neural responses to mounting, intromission, and male ejaculation. Some preoptic cells showed prolonged activity after ejaculation, when subsequent female sexual motivation was reduced. Calcium imaging associated particular cellular activity patterns with events in the interaction rather than assuming one signal represented the entire mating episode.

Excitatory and inhibitory neurons did not all follow the same response profile. The identity and timing of the responding population helped distinguish the sensory event from the longer behavioral state that followed. A brief interaction can thus leave a neural state that affects later willingness to re-enter the mating situation.

slides.title: Activating a mating-tagged ensemble suppresses behavior
body: The female preoptic study used activity-dependent labeling to identify neurons recruited during mating-related events. **An ensemble** is a group of neurons whose activity is considered together because they participate in a common event or state. Labeling provided a way to manipulate cells selected by their previous activity rather than only by anatomical position.

Activating a labeled preoptic subpopulation suppressed subsequent female sexual behavior under the tested conditions. The intervention moved beyond observing a correlation between activity and reduced motivation. It showed that driving part of the event-associated population could alter the later behavioral response in an established social circuit.

This result does not mean that all medial preoptic neurons suppress mating. Other populations contribute to motivation, performance, and parental behavior. The effect depended on which cells were labeled and activated, illustrating how anatomically neighboring neurons can promote different phases or opposing components of the same broad behavioral domain.

slides.title: Ventromedial hypothalamic circuits help regulate receptivity
body: The **ventromedial hypothalamus**, or VMH, contains hormone-sensitive populations important for female rodent mating responses. Estradiol and progesterone change the responsiveness of this network. Sensory information from social investigation and physical contact can then influence the descending pathways that organize receptive posture and related actions.

In classic rat experiments, VMH damage prevented normal lordosis even with ovarian hormone treatment, while stimulation could facilitate the response. These findings distinguished an available hormone signal from the intact neural tissue needed to translate it into behavior. Hormone administration could not simply bypass the loss of the relevant circuit.

Descending VMH influences interact with midbrain and spinal motor pathways. Genital and flank stimulation also provide feedback during the interaction. A receptive posture therefore reflects hormone-dependent readiness combined with the appropriate sensory event and motor circuitry, rather than estrogen acting directly on every muscle participating in the response.

slides.title: Sex-determining genes can specify parts of a social circuit
body: In fruit flies, **doublesex** and **fruitless** regulate development and function of sex-biased neural populations. These genes influence transcription rather than circulating as steroid hormones. A study used genetic intersections to select neurons expressing particular combinations of these regulators and then tested the behavior produced when those cells were activated.

The investigators distinguished neurons contributing to the ability to execute courtship from mechanisms that enhance courtship toward females. Activating defined populations could produce courtship actions toward different targets. The execution of a motor pattern and its direction toward a particular kind of social stimulus were therefore partly separable properties of the circuit.

Fly genetic tools allow precise tests of neurons whose developmental identity is controlled by sex-determining genes. These experiments concern a species-specific reproductive circuit. The labels used for a fly’s target-directed courtship should not be treated as direct equivalents of human gender identity, attraction, or the social meaning of a relationship.

slides.title: Courtship execution and target selection are separable
body: The fruit-fly study altered fruitless function while preserving the doublesex-dependent component of a selected neural population. The manipulation tested whether an animal retained the machinery needed to perform courtship when the usual enhancement toward females was changed. It separated a developmental regulator from the complete disappearance of every courtship-related neuron.

The researchers found distinct contributions to courtship capability and female-directed enhancement, with cooperative regulation in other neuronal subclasses. Related populations could also influence aggression toward males under different genetic and stimulation conditions. A genetically specified social circuit therefore contained interacting components rather than one neuron group encoding every aspect of biological sex.

An observed action can be decomposed into the sensory target, the internal drive, and the available motor program. Changing one component need not abolish all the others. This circuit logic explains why a genetic manipulation can preserve an action while changing when or toward which stimulus that action is expressed.

slides.title: Sex-related brain variation depends on the feature measured
body: **Sexual dimorphism** describes an average difference between groups in a biological trait. It does not mean every individual falls into two nonoverlapping categories for that trait. Brain volume, receptor expression, cell number, and gene transcription are different measurements and can show different patterns within the same species.

A larger structure is not automatically more active or better at a psychological function. Regional volume can reflect several cellular and anatomical contributors. Establishing a behavioral mechanism requires evidence about the relevant cells, their signals, and their effects rather than inferring function directly from a group-average anatomical difference.

Individual developmental histories also differ across hormonal, genetic, and environmental conditions. Consequently, an anatomical measurement does not establish a person’s gender identity or sexual orientation. Such psychological characteristics require their own descriptions and measurements rather than being assigned from an average difference observed in a brain image.

slides.title: Human and mouse brain differences do not match uniformly
body: A comparative MRI study examined sex-related variation in human and mouse brain anatomy. **Magnetic resonance imaging**, or MRI, measures tissue-related signals that can be used to estimate regional volumes. The researchers compared homologous regions, structures judged to correspond across species, instead of assuming that any similarly named region had identical sex effects.

Human males had larger and more variable total brain volume on average, but the same pattern was not mirrored in mice. Adjusting regional measurements for total volume changed the question from overall size to regional organization. The comparison revealed only modest agreement across corresponding structures rather than a uniform cross-species anatomical rule.

This matters when selecting an animal model for a particular developmental mechanism. A mouse region can help test cellular processes, but its group difference may be retained, reduced, or reversed in humans. The appropriate comparison depends on the actual anatomical feature being studied rather than on a general claim that one species reproduces every human sex difference.

slides.title: Group averages differ from individual variation
body: The comparative MRI study also examined variability within groups and patterns of regional anatomy. An average difference summarizes the centers of two distributions, while variability describes their spread. Two groups can differ in their average measurement while many individuals have overlapping values, making a single person difficult to characterize from that feature.

Cross-species agreement was stronger in some cortical regions than in other brain territories. Regional gene-expression comparisons provided another level of analysis, but anatomical agreement and molecular similarity were not interchangeable. The researchers measured whether related patterns occurred rather than demonstrating that one gene directly caused a particular human behavior.

Anatomical observations are therefore most informative when the species, region, scaling method, and measured trait are specified. They can guide experiments on development without functioning as psychological classification tests. The study did not provide a method for identifying a person’s orientation or gender from a structural brain scan.

slides.title: Sex traits, gender identity, and orientation are distinct
body: **Gender identity** concerns a person’s experienced gender, while **sexual orientation** concerns patterns of attraction. Neither is identical to chromosomes, genital anatomy, hormone concentration, or a particular sexual action. These characteristics can be related in someone’s life while still describing different biological, psychological, and social dimensions.

**Sexual behavior** records what someone does, whereas attraction describes whom they desire and identity describes how they understand or describe themselves. Studies sometimes measure only one of these dimensions. A result obtained from a question about past behavior should not automatically be reported as a complete explanation of every dimension of orientation.

Development includes interacting genetic, endocrine, experiential, and social processes whose contributions vary across traits. Human diversity cannot be reduced to a single brain region or hormone level. Describing the measured characteristic precisely preserves the difference between a population-level developmental finding and an unsupported prediction about an individual person.

slides.title: Orientation develops through multiple interacting influences
body: Research on sexual orientation examines genetic variation, prenatal environments, developmental history, and reported attraction or behavior. **Heritability** describes the contribution of genetic differences to variation within a studied population under particular conditions. It does not specify the fraction of an individual’s orientation that is genetic or establish a single determining gene.

Clinical variations in prenatal hormone signaling have contributed evidence about development, but outcomes differ among individuals. Such findings are informative about particular pathways and exposures rather than being deterministic tests. A hormone-sensitive developmental process can influence a probability without fixing every later preference, identity, or life experience.

Twin comparisons, endocrine observations, and anatomical studies also measure different levels of biology. Agreement among relatives can be informative without making their experiences identical, and group-average anatomy does not identify an individual’s attraction. A multifactorial account preserves these distinct observations rather than forcing them into one universal developmental pathway.

slides.title: Adult hormones do not diagnose sexual orientation
body: An adult blood sample describes a current endocrine state, not the complete hormonal environment experienced during brain development. Hormone levels also vary with time of day, health, medication, age, and reproductive condition. A present-day concentration therefore cannot reconstruct a person’s prenatal neural development or establish the origin of their attraction.

Likewise, an experimental change in sexual motivation is not the same as changing orientation. Hormones can affect the strength of interest or aspects of physiological function while attraction remains directed toward the same partners. The dependent variable must remain the one actually measured rather than being expanded into a different psychological claim.

Human sexual and gender diversity are not disease categories requiring a neural explanation to justify their existence. Neuroscience can investigate development and variation without treating a normal identity as a defect. Biological findings explain processes and distributions; they do not supply a hierarchy of legitimate identities or desirable patterns of attraction.

slides.title: Pair bonding requires recognizing and valuing a partner
body: A **pair bond** is a selective, enduring social attachment to a particular partner. It requires more than recognizing that another animal is present. Sensory information must identify the individual, while memory and motivation give interactions with that individual a different value from interactions with an unfamiliar conspecific.

Prairie voles provide one laboratory model because paired animals often prefer familiar partners in controlled contact tests. These assays measure selective affiliation rather than every aspect of human attachment. Related vole species differ in social organization, helping researchers examine which neural and receptor differences accompany particular patterns of bonding.

Oxytocin, vasopressin, dopamine, and other signals can influence bonding-related networks through particular receptors and brain regions. Their effects depend on experience and experimental conditions. No single peptide should be described as containing a complete representation of the partner or mechanically producing every feature of a lasting relationship.

slides.title: Reward and memory contribute to partner preference
body: The **nucleus accumbens** and **ventral pallidum** participate in motivated behavior and the value of social interactions. In vole experiments, neuropeptide and dopamine manipulations in these networks can alter the development or expression of partner preference. These effects connect individual recognition to the motivation to seek or maintain contact.

**Vasopressin** and **oxytocin** act through different receptors whose distribution varies across species and brain regions. Changing receptor availability can alter the effect of a social encounter. A circulating peptide concentration consequently does not describe how strongly every bonding-related target is responding at the synaptic level.

Bonding also has phases: initial attraction, repeated interaction, selective affiliation, and responses to separation. A manipulation can affect one phase more than another. Measuring partner contact after a defined pairing period tests a specific part of this process rather than demonstrating that an animal has acquired every component of an enduring social bond.

slides.title: Pair formation recruits coordinated brain-wide activity
body: A prairie-vole study used whole-brain imaging to map **c-Fos**, a protein whose expression often increases after neuronal activation. The investigators compared pairing conditions and time points to identify patterns associated with mating and bond formation. c-Fos mapping integrates activity over time rather than reporting the moment-by-moment electrical firing of each cell.

Bonding-related activity involved networks spanning hypothalamic, amygdalar, reward, and cortical regions. Patterns were coordinated across the members of a pair and were strongly related to their mating interactions. The findings extended beyond one isolated bonding nucleus to circuits involved in social sensation, reproductive behavior, reward, and territorial responses.

Males and females showed substantial similarity in these coordinated patterns rather than entirely separate bonding systems. The atlas made it possible to compare the same anatomical locations across animals. Activity mapping identified candidate networks for later causal experiments without establishing that every c-Fos-positive cell was individually necessary for forming a bond.

For each voxel, an analysis of variance (ANOVA) test was used to compare null and hypothesized GLMs. False discovery rate (FDR)  q -values were computed from the ANOVA results to account for multiple comparisons across voxels (alpha threshold of q = 0.1). False discovery rate (FDR)  q -values were computed to adjust for multiple comparisons acros ROIs (alpha threshold of  q  = 0.1). The most significant ROIs per cluster are labeled with the symbol size scaled by the  F -statistic. Darkness and thickness of connecting lines reflect Pearson correlation coefficients. ( E ) Time course trajectories of total c-Fos+ cell counts are shown for each cluster. Red lines represent mates and blue lines represent siblings (females – lighter, males – darker). In ( C ,  D ,  E ), each cluster group is given a label to summarize the most significant ROIs within it. slides.title: Separation changes molecules before preference fades
body: A prairie-vole study compared behavior and nucleus-accumbens gene expression after partner separation. **RNA sequencing** measures the abundance of gene transcripts in a tissue sample. It can reveal changes in molecular state without directly measuring whether an individual neuron fires more often or whether the animal still prefers its familiar partner.

After prolonged separation, some pair-bond-associated transcriptional patterns weakened even though partner-directed affiliation remained detectable. Molecular adaptation and the measured social preference therefore followed different time courses. The absence of one transcript pattern did not mean that every behavioral feature of the bond had already disappeared.

The researchers also enriched RNA from neurons to distinguish neuronal changes from patterns in the mixed tissue. Different analyses implicated cellular maintenance, signaling, and glial-related processes. The result concerns a vole’s adaptation to separation and provides possible biological targets without equating that molecular process with the complete human experience of grief.

Original figure legend: Figure 3. Prolonged separation erodes pair bond transcriptional signatures. ( A ) Opposite-sex and same-sex pairs were paired for 2 weeks prior to a baseline partner preference test. Pairs were then separated for either 48 hours (short-term) or 4 weeks (long-term) prior to collecting fresh nucleus accumbens tissue for RNAseq. Animals in the Remain Paired group are analyzed in  Figure 2  to define the Combined Pair Bond transcriptional signature. ( B ) Baseline partner preference scores of males included in RNA sequencing for the opposite- and same-sex separation groups (one-tailed t-test relative to 50%: opposite-sex T 11 =11.56, p=1.71 X 10 –7 ; same-sex T 9 =6.07, p=1.87 X 10 –4 ). Black dotted line indicates a 50% partner preference score and the grey dotted line indicates 66%. There were no differences in partner preference score between opposite-sex and same-sex separated animals used for RNAseq (two-tailed t-test: T 14.33  = 0.33, p=0.75). ( C ) Transcriptional analysis workflow similar to  Figure 2 . ( D ) Heatmap of the scaled log 2 FoldChange for every gene where short- and long-term separation is compared to the combined pair bond gene signature. ( E ) RRHO using the combined pair bond, short-term separated, and long-term separated ranked transcript lists show that short-term separated animals retain a gene expression pattern concordant with pair bond transcription while there is a dramatic erosion of pair bond gene expression following long-term separation. ( F, G ) Upset plot showing overlap of genes in the UU or DD quadrants of  2F  and  3E  RRHO was determined using a Fisher’s Exact test. The difference between the intersections of the pair-bond:short-term sep. and pair-bond:long-term sep. was used to define the eroded gene lists. ( H, I ) The RRHO gene lists of eroded pair bond genes were used to filter the DESeq heatmap in  2D . Eroded genes from the UU quadrants show upregulation during pair bonding and short-term separation but downregulation after long-term separation ( H ) while the eroded genes from the DD quadrants show the opposite pattern ( I ). ( J, K ) GO and IPA analysis of RRHO quadrant gene lists and pair bond eroded gene lists. Scale represents the –log 10 (p-adjusted) where any non-significant terms are white. ( J ) Glial associated GO terms of the UU quadrants are less significantly represented after separation and are highly significantly represented among the eroded genes. Significant upstream regulators of the eroded genes include Sox2, estrogen receptor, Erbb3, and Ctnnb1. ( K ) Vesicle docking and synapse organization associated GO terms of the DD quadrants are less significantly represented after separation and are more significantly represented among the pair bond eroded genes. Significant upstream regulators of the eroded genes include Hnf4a, Calmodulin, Hdac4, and Adora2a.

slides.title: Parental care solves several different problems for offspring
body: Newborn rodents depend on adults for warmth, nutrition, grooming, and protection. **Pup retrieval** returns a displaced infant to the nest, while nursing supplies milk and huddling helps conserve heat. These behaviors solve different physiological problems, so one successful retrieval does not establish that every component of care is functioning normally.

An adult must detect infant cues, approach without attacking, handle the pup appropriately, and return it to a suitable location. The sequence combines sensory recognition, motivation, and coordinated movement. A deficit can arise at any of these steps rather than reflecting a complete loss of every response to an infant.

Caregiving is not restricted to the biological mother in every species or situation. Fathers and other adults can care for offspring under appropriate conditions. The neural mechanisms must therefore support flexible responses to infant needs rather than requiring pregnancy as an unavoidable prerequisite for every form of parental action.

slides.title: Pregnancy and experience both prepare caregiving
body: During pregnancy and birth, changes in progesterone, estradiol, prolactin, and oxytocin alter reproductive and caregiving systems. **Prolactin** contributes to milk production, while **oxytocin** promotes milk ejection and acts within social circuits. These are distinct functions: producing milk and releasing it to the infant require different biological steps.

In rodent experiments, hormonal conditions around birth facilitate the onset of maternal behavior. Repeated exposure to pups can also promote care in adults that have not undergone pregnancy. Endocrine preparation and experience therefore provide partially different routes for making infant cues effective at recruiting caregiving responses.

Once care has been learned, the hormonal requirements for its expression can differ from those for its initial acquisition. The relevant experiment must specify whether it tests the first appearance, later maintenance, or a particular component of behavior. A hormone that accelerates learning need not be required identically for every subsequent retrieval.

slides.title: A growth-factor signal contributes to maternal behavior
body: **Brain-derived neurotrophic factor**, or BDNF, is a protein signal that regulates neuronal development and plasticity. Different gene promoters can produce BDNF transcripts encoding the same protein. A mouse study disrupted particular promoter-driven expression patterns to ask whether the source and developmental regulation of this signal affected female social behavior.

Females with the relevant BDNF deficits showed impaired maternal care and reduced sexual receptivity. Their hypothalamic oxytocin expression was also reduced during development. The changes linked a growth-factor pathway to a neuropeptide system, while leaving open which cellular effects contributed to each distinct behavioral deficit.

The study measured specific caregiving actions rather than assigning a single global parenting score as the entire mechanism. A molecular alteration can affect how an adult approaches or handles pups without changing every movement or sensory ability. Such component measurements help locate the behavioral consequences of a developmental signaling disturbance.

BDNF-TrkB signaling in oxytocin neurons contributes to maternal behavior. eLife. https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.33676

Original figure legend: 10.7554/eLife.33676.002 Figure 1. Disruption of BDNF from promoters I and II leads to impaired maternal care. ( a ) Schematic of  Bdnf  transcript production. Transcription is initiated from promoters upstream of individual 5’-untranslated regions (UTRs) and spliced to the common coding exon IX. Each transcript produces an identical BDNF protein. ( b ) Design of Bdnf -/- mice using Bdnf-e1 -/- as a representative example. Targeting vectors were designed to insert an enhanced green fluorescent protein (eGFP) upstream of the exon’s splice donor site. Bdnf-e1 -/- mice express a  Bdnf -I-eGFP-STOP- Bdnf  IX transcript leading to the production of GFP in lieu of BDNF. ( c ) Average litter size over time for WT, Bdnf-e1 -/-, and Bdnf-e2 -/- postpartum mothers exposed to the pup retrieval test one day after giving birth. Bdnf-e1 -/- mothers show significant pup loss compared to WT mothers (2-way ANOVA with mixed effect model; p<0.001). ( d ) Average litter size over time for WT and Bdnf-e1 -/- postpartum mothers remaining in the homecage. Bdnf-e1 -/- mothers show significant pup loss compared to WT mothers even in a naturalistic setting (2-way ANOVA with mixed effect model; p<0.001). ( e ) Percentage of postpartum mothers losing their entire litter by postnatal day 3 (P3). Approximately 1/3 of postpartum Bdnf-e1 -/- mothers lose their entire litter by P3 (1-way ANOVA with Bonferroni’s multiple comparisons; p<0.05). ( f ) Proportion of WT, Bdnf-e1 -/- and Bdnf-e2 -/- with different maternal types including parenting (P), disorganized parenting (DP), partial parenting (PP), disorganized partial parenting (DPP), and non-parenting (NP). There is a significant decrease in the proportion of Bdnf-e1 -/- postpartum mothers with parenting behavior compared to WT (one-tailed Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon rank sum test, p<0.05). Bdnf-e1 -/- postpartum mothers show corresponding elevations in non-parenting behaviors. ( g ) Bar graph depicting nest building behavior before parturition. Bdnf-e1 and -e2 -/- show impaired nest building compared to WT (Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn’s multiple comparisons, p<0.01). ( h–j ) Latency to first retrieval ( h ) time carrying first pup ( i ) and time nesting with first pup ( j ) during the pup retrieval test. Bdnf-e1 -/- postpartum mothers show increased latency to retrieval, longer time carrying the first pup to the nest, and reduced nesting time with first pup (1-way ANOVA with Bonferroni’s multiple comparisons, p<0.05). Bdnf-e2 -/- postpartum mothers show similar, albeit milder phenotypes. ( k ) Percentage of postpartum mothers successfully retrieving all pups and nesting for at least 2 continuous minutes. Significantly fewer Bdnf-e1 -/- postpartum mothers successfully retrieve pups and continuously nest compared to WT (1-way ANOVA with Bonferroni’s multiple comparisons, p<0.05). ( l ) Bar graph depicting nest building behavior of WT and Bdnf-e1virgins 24 hr prior to pup retrieval test. Bdnf-e1 -/- virgins show impairments in nest building compared to WT virgins (Mann-Whitney test, p<0.05). ( m–o ) Maternal ( m ), abnormal parenting ( n ) and retrieval ( o ) indices for WT and Bdnf-e1 -/- virgins during foreign pup retrieval test. Bdnf-e1 -/- virgin females show reductions in maternal and retrieval indices and a strong trend for increased abnormal parenting (Mann-Whitney tests, p<0.01, p<0.05, and p=0.0529, respectively). ( p ) Proportion of WT and Bdnf-e1 -/- virgin females with different maternal types including parenting ( P ) partial parenting (PP), irregular parenting (IP), non-parenting (NP), and attack (A). There is a significant decrease in the proportion of Bdnf-e1 -/- virgins with parenting behavior compared to WT. Bdnf-e1 -/- virgins show corresponding elevations in attack behavior (one-tailed Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon rank sum test, p<0.05). Data are means ± SEM. (n = 16 WT postpartum mothers; n = 22 Bdnf-e1 -/- postpartum mothers; n = 17 Bdnf-e2 -/- postpartum mothers; n = 12 WT virgins; n = 12 Bdnf-e1 -/- virgins; *p<0.05, **p<0.01, and p<0.001, #p<0.0001).

slides.title: Oxytocin neurons also depend on the signals they receive
body: BDNF acts through **TrkB**, a receptor that changes intracellular signaling after binding the growth factor. The maternal-behavior study removed TrkB selectively from oxytocin neurons. This manipulation tested the receiving side of the pathway rather than reducing BDNF everywhere in the brain or eliminating every oxytocin-producing cell.

The receptor manipulation reproduced part of the maternal-care impairment seen with broader BDNF disruption. The result indicated that BDNF signaling within oxytocin neurons contributed to normal caregiving responses. It did not imply that oxytocin neurons were the only BDNF targets involved in every reproductive or social effect.

Cell-enriched RNA measurements identified molecular pathways related to neuronal structure and plasticity in the oxytocin population. A cell that releases a social peptide is therefore also regulated by developmental and trophic inputs. Changes in those inputs can alter how that neuron develops and functions before its peptide is released to downstream targets.

slides.title: Preoptic caregiving circuits compete with infant avoidance
body: The medial preoptic area helps coordinate parental responses to infant cues. In rodent experiments, damage to this region can disrupt retrieval and other aspects of care. Its projections interact with motivational and motor systems, allowing a pup’s sensory features to recruit an organized approach and handling response.

Other pathways can promote avoidance or attack, particularly in animals whose current social and reproductive state does not favor care. Parental behavior therefore involves both facilitating appropriate actions and reducing competing responses. An infant cue does not carry an invariant command that produces the same behavior in every adult encountering it.

Cell-specific research has identified galanin-expressing preoptic neurons that participate in parenting in both sexes. Their manipulation can change pup-directed actions, while nearby populations contribute to other social behaviors. The preoptic area is a collection of interacting populations rather than a single center whose activation always produces one complete caregiving sequence.
